Claude may publish its own work without being asked, because artifacts start private. The exception is content that could mislead or cause harm if shared further: anything that imitates a real organization, person or record, and anything the person presented as sensitive. Claude builds those as files and lets the person decide whether they get a URL.

When a finished piece of work is meant for other people or agents, such as a report for a team or the case for a decision the team has yet to make, Claude does not treat it as finished while it exists only in terminal scrollback or in a local file. Claude publishes it, as an Artifact or through a first-party document connector when one is attached, and gives the person the link, so they have a private page ready to share when they choose. Claude publishes it even when the request is phrased as a question, such as "can you write up the plan?". When the request says who else will read or use the work, such as a team, a manager or a reviewer, or where it will be posted or presented, such as a channel or a meeting, Claude publishes it. A write-up that will be posted in a channel or a thread is still published, so the post can carry the link; when it is short, Claude also gives the text in its reply, ready to paste. When it might be passed along but nothing says so, Claude offers the page in one line instead of saying nothing. When the person asks only for Claude's own verdict, such as "should we ship this?", and names no one else who will read it, Claude gives the answer in the terminal and offers the page in one line instead of publishing it. A recommendation or analysis written up for someone else to act on is finished work for that reader, so Claude publishes it. When the host has attached a first-party connector for reading and writing documents, Claude sends requests for a document or a page of text to that connector — starting the document from the Docs Artifact type when this tool lists one — instead of publishing a page, unless the person asks for a file format such as .docx or .pptx. **Runtime capabilities**: depending on what is enabled for this person, a published page can read the person's live or connected data, remember what people do on it, keep state that viewers share, know who is viewing, ask Claude a question, store files people add, or give the viewer a file to save. action.description: One of 'publish', 'list', 'read', 'delete', 'open', 'pin', 'unpin', 'quickstart'. Omitting it means 'publish'. **Calls** in the description says what each one does and takes, except as noted here.

file_path.description: publish: the local page Claude publishes (.html, or .md only when a skill says so). For an Artifact created from an Artifact type, it is one of that Artifact's data files. With `asset: true`, it is the local file Claude uploads. A short, distinctive basename also serves as the title when nothing else gives one.

asset.description: publish with `url`: true uploads `file_path` (or each of `file_paths`) to that artifact's asset store instead of publishing it as the page — or, with `from_url` and `asset_ids` in place of `file_path`, copies those assets of another artifact into it server side (see **Calls**).

file_paths.description: publish with `asset: true` only: several local image, video, PDF, font, stylesheet or script files in place of `file_path`, up to 25 in one call, all into the artifact that `url` names; one approval covers the call, and the result lists each file's id and url, or why it was not uploaded. A CSV, Markdown, JSON or plain-text file, a symbolic or hard link, and a file outside the working directory each go in a call of their own with `file_path`.

from_url.description: publish with `asset: true`, in place of `file_path`: the SOURCE artifact's claude.ai URL — one the person can open.

asset_ids.description: publish with `asset: true` and `from_url` only: 1–10 distinct asset ids from the source artifact (from a `scope: "assets"` listing of it, or an upload result).

favicon.description: Deprecated; Claude omits it and uses `icon`.

icon.description: One short generic word for the artifact's browser-tab icon, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map: a plain signifier, never a product or brand name. Claude includes it on every page's first publish and omits it on a redeploy so the artifact keeps its icon, passing a new one only when the person asks. Ignored on an Artifact created from an Artifact type.

files.description: Supporting files to publish alongside the page, as a map {"published/path": "source/path" | {from, contentType} | {artifact, path, ver?} | null}. The key is what the HTML references. The source is a path on disk, or {from, contentType} when the type cannot be inferred from the published extension. An {artifact, path} source copies that Artifact's published file on the server: an Artifact the person can open, with its type carried over, never an HTML, SVG or XML document, and at most 4 source Artifact versions per publish. null removes that path on an update, and files left out are kept. A plain list publishes each file at its own spelling. Sources must be under the working directory or Claude's scratchpad directory. `preflight.js` at the artifact root is reserved: it runs against open pages when Claude publishes updates, and it must be a JavaScript module of at most 8 KiB whose default export is a function, or the publish is refused.

path.description: Path relative to the working directory (or to `root`, which may be a folder in your scratchpad directory); the file is served at this same path next to the page.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the extension for common types (css/js/json/png/…) — pass explicitly otherwise.

from.description: Source file path — relative to `root` (default: the working directory), or absolute under the working directory or your scratchpad directory.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the PUBLISHED extension for common types — pass explicitly otherwise.

artifact.description: Another artifact's claude.ai URL: the file is copied from ITS published files, server side — nothing is downloaded. You must be able to open that artifact.

path.description: The file's published path inside that Artifact, as a listing of its files prints it (not "index.html").

ver.description: A version of that Artifact to copy from instead of its current one — only versions you are served (its history, if you can edit it); omit for the current version.

root.description: The base directory that relative `files` sources resolve against, like a bundler root. It never changes published paths. It is relative to the working directory, or absolute within it or within Claude's scratchpad directory. It requires `files`, except on an Artifact made from a type, where a data `file_path` under it is served at its path relative to it.

pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all', 'types', 'files' (with `url`) and 'assets' (with `url`, continued with `after`). See **Calls**.

type_query.description: list with scope 'types' only: limits the listing to the types whose title or description match this text best, ignoring case; a type that matches less well is left out, so a narrowed listing is not the whole catalog. Claude omits it when choosing a type for a request, unless a listing made without it says more types exist than it shows.

type.description: list only: the name of a published Artifact type, as a 'types' listing shows it (case does not matter). The listing then shows the Artifacts made from that type instead of the person's gallery. Claude passes this or `type_url`, not both.

intent.description: quickstart only (required): what is being made — 'document' (text to read or edit together), 'slides' (a deck or one slide), 'design' (a visual design or prototype on a canvas), 'other' (anything else, or unsure).

design_systems.description: quickstart only: false when a design system's link is already in hand (it is then read with its own call) or one was declined. Omitted or true, the result lists the design systems (not for a document) and, for slides or a design, attaches the default one's README.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys. On a `type_url` create, it is the new Artifact's name: what the person called it, or a short descriptive name. If it is left out, the Artifact is named after the type.

description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

overwrite_unread.description: publish with `files` or `root` to an existing artifact: published paths this call may replace or remove although you have not read or listed them in this session. Every other path the call touches must be one you read by its `path`, saw in a file listing, or published yourself, and must not have changed since — otherwise nothing is sent and the refusal names each path. Name a path here only when the user asked for it to be replaced without looking at what is there; it never excuses a path that changed after you read it.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai URL. On a publish, it is the artifact to update in place, which must be one the person owns or was given edit access to (a read of it says "writer"); Claude omits it for a new artifact or a redeploy in the same conversation (see **To update an artifact from an earlier conversation**). For read, delete and the other calls that take a URL, it is the artifact to act on.

type_url.description: publish: the Artifact type to create this new, private Artifact from (a link from a 'types' listing). Claude omits `url`. Any `file_path`/`files` passed become the new Artifact's own files beside the type's fixed ones. read (no `url`): the type to describe. list: the type whose Artifacts to list, or Claude names the type with `type` instead.

auto_open.description: Only with `type_url` and no `file_path`: when the new Artifact opens for the person. Claude passes "after_first_write" when it will fill the Artifact right after creating it with a files publish to its url, so the person does not first see it empty. The Artifact then opens on that first write. Otherwise Claude omits it, and the Artifact opens when created; Claude always omits it for a type whose content it writes through a connector, such as a Claude Docs document, since no publish or store write follows to open it.

prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

content.text:
I read all five files in `src/gateway`, plus the pieces they depend on (`KlerosCore`, `xKlerosLiquidV2`, `Constants`, `SafeERC20`, the deploy scripts and the relayer bot). Note: `node_modules` isn't installed, so I could not read the actual Vea outbox implementation — my statements about Vea's `sendMessage` semantics are based on `mock/VeaMock.sol` and the interfaces, and I flag where that matters.

## How the pair works

Two contracts on two chains, connected by Vea (an optimistic bridge). Neither one does arbitration — they are an adapter that makes KlerosCore on Arbitrum look like a local `IArbitratorV2` to a contract on Ethereum or Gnosis.

- **`ForeignGateway`** (Ethereum / Gnosis) pretends to be an arbitrator. It takes ETH, mints a local `disputeID`, and emits an event. It never talks to Vea outbound — it only *receives*.
- **`HomeGateway`** (Arbitrum) pretends to be an arbitrable. It creates the real dispute on KlerosCore, and receives `rule()` back from KlerosCore, which it forwards into the Vea inbox.
- **The relayer** is an off-chain bot (`scripts/disputeRelayerBot.ts`) that watches the foreign chain and pays the home-chain arbitration fee out of its own pocket, expecting reimbursement at the very end.

The only thing linking the two sides is `disputeHash` — a keccak of the creation parameters, computed independently on both chains and expected to match. There is no proof carried across on the outbound leg at all.

## Flow of a message

**Outbound (dispute creation) — no bridge involved:**

1. Arbitrable calls `ForeignGateway.createDispute{value}(choices, extraData)` (`ForeignGateway.sol:148`). Cost is checked against a **locally mirrored** `feeForJuror[courtID]`, not against KlerosCore.
2. `disputeID = localDisputeID++` (starts at 1), and `disputeHash = keccak256("createDispute", blockhash(block.number-1), chainID, msg.sender, disputeID, choices, extraData)` (`:159`).
3. `DisputeData{id, arbitrable, paid: msg.value, relayer: 0, ruled: false}` stored; `CrossChainDisputeOutgoing` emitted (`:179`). **The ETH just sits in the ForeignGateway.**
4. The bot sees the event, *also scrapes the arbitrable's `DisputeRequest` log from the same tx* to recover `templateId` (`disputeRelayerBot.ts:85-96`), and calls `HomeGateway.relayCreateDispute(params)` on Arbitrum, **paying the real fee itself**.
5. `HomeGateway` recomputes the same hash (`HomeGateway.sol:145`), rejects a duplicate via `relayedData.relayer != 0`, calls `arbitrator.createDispute{value: msg.value}`, records `disputeID ↔ hash` both ways, and stamps `relayer = msg.sender`.

So the "message" on the outbound leg is a social/economic construct: an untrusted bot re-typing parameters into a hash function on the other chain. If the hash doesn't match, nothing breaks loudly — the dispute just becomes an orphan that reverts on the return leg.

**Inbound (ruling) — this is the only real bridged message:**

6. Jurors vote; `KlerosCore.executeRuling` calls `dispute.arbitrated.rule(...)` → `HomeGateway.rule` (`HomeGateway.sol:229`).
7. It looks up the hash and calls `veaInbox.sendMessage(foreignGateway, IForeignGateway.relayRule.selector, abi.encode(disputeHash, ruling, relayer))`. Note `_messageSender` is deliberately omitted — Vea splices it in (`:235-239`).
8. Vea snapshots, an epoch passes, a claim is made and (optimistically) not challenged.
9. Someone relays on Ethereum: the Vea outbox calls `ForeignGateway.relayRule(homeGatewayAddr, hash, ruling, relayer)`. `onlyFromVea` checks both the outbox address (current, or the deprecated one inside its grace window) and that the origin sender is `homeGateway` (`ForeignGateway.sol:55-63`).
10. `ruled = true`, `relayer` recorded, then `arbitrable.rule(dispute.id, ruling)` (`:227`).
11. Separately, the relayer calls `withdrawFees(hash)` and gets `dispute.paid` back (`:232`).

Total latency foreign→home is bot-speed; home→foreign is a full Vea epoch plus challenge window. The relayer's capital is locked from step 4 to step 11 — the whole dispute lifetime — with zero premium.

## Concerns

Ordered by how much they'd worry me.

**1. The fee mirror can silently price disputes at zero, and its fallback disagrees with KlerosCore.**

`ForeignGateway.extraDataToCourtIDMinJurors` (`:267-283`) does:

```solidity
if (feeForJuror[courtID] == 0) courtID = 0;
```

KlerosCore does the opposite (`KlerosCore.sol:1517`): unknown or forking court → `GENERAL_COURT` (1). And `feeForJuror[0]` is never set — both deploy scripts set only `Courts.GENERAL` and leave `// TODO: set up the correct fees for the FORKING_COURT` (`deploy/01-foreign-gateway-on-ethereum.ts:47-50`, same on Gnosis).

So for any court without a mirrored fee, `arbitrationCost` returns `0 * minJurors = 0`. Anyone can open a dispute on the foreign chain for free, and the home chain would charge the real General Court fee. No relayer will ever touch it, so it isn't a theft vector — it's a free-DoS/orphan-dispute vector, and the arbitrable is left hanging with no ruling. Fixing the fallback to mirror KlerosCore (`→ GENERAL_COURT`) and reverting when the resolved fee is 0 would close it.

The broader version of this: the mirror is maintained by hand (`changeCourtJurorFee` appears only in deploy scripts — no sync bot in the repo). Any upward change to a court's `feeForJuror` on Arbitrum immediately makes already-created foreign disputes unprofitable to relay.

**2. There is no refund, cancel, or timeout on the foreign side.**

`withdrawFees` requires `dispute.ruled` (`:235`), and `ruled` is only ever set by `relayRule`. If a dispute is never relayed — underpriced per above, court doesn't support the dispute kit (`KlerosCore._createDispute` reverts on `DisputeKitNotSupportedByCourt`), arbitration paused, or simply no bot running — the ETH is stuck in the ForeignGateway permanently. There's no owner rescue either. The deploy script itself flags this: *"TODO: disable the gateway until fully initialized with the correct fees OR allow disputeCreators to add funds again if necessary."* Given an upgradeable proxy you can patch it later, but today there's no escape hatch.

**3. `templateId` is not covered by the disputeHash.**

`disputeHash` binds blockhash, chainID, arbitrable, disputeID, choices, extraData (`HomeGateway.sol:145-155`) — but `_params.templateId` is passed straight to `emit DisputeRequest` / `CrossChainDisputeIncoming` (`:164-173`) without ever being committed to. The relayer is untrusted and picked by a race. A malicious relayer can relay the genuine dispute with an arbitrary `templateId`, so **the jurors read a dispute description of the relayer's choosing** while the resulting ruling still binds the real arbitrable, and the attacker still collects the reimbursement. The honest `templateId` is only recoverable off-chain by scraping the arbitrable's `DisputeRequest` log on the foreign chain (which is exactly what the bot does, but nothing on-chain enforces it). Folding `templateId` into the hash preimage on both sides is cheap and closes this.

**4. `relayRule` couples bookkeeping to an untrusted external call.**

```solidity
dispute.ruled = true;
dispute.relayer = _relayer;
arbitrable.rule(dispute.id, _ruling);   // UNTRUSTED
```

The state write ordering is right (no reentrancy issue), but if `arbitrable.rule()` reverts or burns all gas, the whole Vea relay tx reverts. If the Vea outbox marks the message relayed only on success (which is what I'd expect, and what `VeaMock` implies with its `require(success, "Call failure")`), the message can be retried — but a *permanently* reverting arbitrable means the ruling is never delivered, `ruled` is never set, and **the relayer's principal is locked forever.** That's a 1:1 griefing cost for a malicious arbitrable: burn your own fee to burn the relayer's. Worse, a conditionally-reverting arbitrable can censor rulings it dislikes. `try/catch` around `arbitrable.rule` with a fixed gas stipend, so the ruling is recorded regardless of delivery, would decouple reimbursement from arbitrable behaviour. I'd want this one confirmed against the real `VeaOutboxArbToEth` before acting.

**5. Governance setters break in-flight disputes, and one of them can cross wires.**

`changeArbitrator` (`HomeGateway.sol:109`) is the worst: `rule()` gates on `msg.sender == address(arbitrator)`, so every dispute still live on the old core becomes permanently unrulable. And `disputeIDtoHash` is keyed by raw core disputeID, which restarts at 0 on a new core — so after a swap, a new dispute with ID *N* overwrites (or reads) the old dispute *N*'s hash, and a ruling can be delivered against the wrong foreign dispute. If `changeArbitrator` is meant to be usable at all, the mapping needs to be namespaced by arbitrator address.

`changeForeignGateway` / `changeHomeGateway` have the milder version: in-flight Vea messages fail `onlyFromVea`'s `_messageSender == homeGateway` check until governance points it back. Recoverable, but there's no grace-period mechanism on that side the way there is for the outbox.

`changeVea` on the foreign side (`ForeignGateway.sol:118`) unconditionally does `deprecatedVeaOutbox = veaOutbox`. Two rotations inside one grace window silently drop the first deprecated outbox's pending messages.

**6. `withdrawFees` uses `.transfer()`.**

`payable(dispute.relayer).transfer(amount)` (`:239`) — 2300 gas. A relayer operating from a Safe or any contract with a non-trivial `receive()` can never be reimbursed, and the funds are permanently stuck since there's no alternative payout path and no way to reassign `relayer`. Also fragile against future gas repricing. `call` with a reentrancy guard (the state is already zeroed first, so it's essentially free) is the standard fix.

**7. Ruling execution on the home chain depends on Vea liveness.**

`KlerosCore.executeRuling` → `HomeGateway.rule` → `veaInbox.sendMessage`. If the inbox reverts for any reason, `executeRuling` reverts, and the home dispute cannot move to a finalized state at all — the failure propagates backwards into core's flow rather than being isolated. Worth deciding deliberately whether that's the behaviour you want.

Also, `rule()` doesn't check `disputeHash != 0` (`:232`); combined with an arbitrator swap it will happily emit a message for the zero hash, which then reverts on the foreign side.

**8. `xKlerosLiquidV2` has a court off-by-one in its cost quote.**

`arbitrationCost` forwards the V1 `_extraData` verbatim to `foreignGateway.arbitrationCost` (`xKlerosLiquidV2.sol:615`), but `createDispute` converts to `subcourtID + 1` before forwarding (`:463-465`). So the quoted price is for the wrong court. It's not exploitable — the ForeignGateway re-checks against the corrected extraData — but a V1 arbitrable that dutifully sends exactly `arbitrationCost()` will have its tx revert, and for the general court (V1 id 0 → `feeForJuror[0] == 0`) it will quote **zero** and always revert.

**Smaller things:**

- `RelayedData.arbitrationCost` (`HomeGateway.sol:29`) is never written or read — dead storage, and the public getter returns a misleading `0`.
- ERC20 path (`:200-203`): `increaseAllowance` without a matching decrease. If the arbitrator ever pulls less than `_feeAmount`, allowance and tokens are stranded with no sweep function.
- `ForeignGateway.currentRuling` reverts unconditionally (`:257`). Any foreign arbitrable written against the full `IArbitratorV2` will break on it.
- The two `relayCreateDispute` overloads are ~40 duplicated lines; the hash computation and the dedupe check should be shared.
- Relayer selection is a pure gas race with no incentive beyond principal return — there's no fee, no tip, and capital is locked for the full dispute duration. That's an economic design choice, but it means the system only works as long as Kleros runs the bot itself.
- Bot nit: `logger.warn("More than 1 DisputeRequest event...")` at `disputeRelayerBot.ts:94` fires unconditionally, outside any check on `disputeRequests.length`.

The ones I'd actually act on first are **1, 2, 3** — they're cheap to fix and two of them are already acknowledged as TODOs in your own deploy scripts.

Want me to write this up as a shareable page, or open issues for the top few?

content.text:
Traced it. `executeRuling` is a plain high-level call with no `try/catch` and no gas cap, so the failure propagates all the way back and reverts the whole transaction.

```
KlerosCore.executeRuling(disputeID)        // KlerosCore.sol:1144, permissionless
  require(!arbitrationPaused)              // :1145
  require(period == execution)             // :1147
  require(!dispute.ruled)                  // :1148
  dispute.ruled = true                     // :1151  ← rolled back
  emit RulingExecuted(...)                 // :1152  ← discarded
  dispute.arbitrated.rule(...)             // :1153  → HomeGateway.rule
      veaInbox.sendMessage(...)            // HomeGateway.sol:239  ← reverts
```

`executeRuling` at `:1144` is the only caller of `arbitrated.rule` in the whole contract, and there is no `try`/`catch` anywhere in `KlerosCore.sol`.

**Immediate effect:** everything rolls back. `dispute.ruled` goes back to `false`, `RulingExecuted` is never emitted. `HomeGateway.rule` writes no state of its own, so there's nothing to unwind there.

**So it's retryable, permissionlessly and indefinitely.** `executeRuling` has no caller restriction and no deadline — the dispute just sits in `Period.execution` (nothing advances past it, there's no timeout) and anyone can call again once the underlying cause is cleared. This is genuinely better than the mirror-image situation on the foreign side in `relayRule`, where retryability depends on whether the Vea outbox already consumed the message.

**Juror payouts are not blocked.** This surprised me a little and is worth knowing: redistribution lives in `execute(disputeID, round, iterations)` at `:909`, which gates only on `Period.execution` and `whenNotPaused` — it never reads `dispute.ruled`. So PNK penalties and fee rewards are distributed normally even if the ruling can never be delivered across the bridge. The dispute is fully settled locally; only the cross-chain leg hangs.

**What stays stuck** is the entire foreign side: the arbitrable never receives `rule()`, and the relayer never gets reimbursed, since `ForeignGateway.withdrawFees` requires `dispute.ruled` (`ForeignGateway.sol:235`) and that flag is only set by `relayRule`. So a `sendMessage` failure locks the relayer's principal for exactly as long as it persists.

**What can actually cause it:**

- **A bad `veaInbox`.** `changeVea` (`HomeGateway.sol:115`) takes any address with no validation. Set it to zero or an EOA and Solidity's `extcodesize` check on the high-level call reverts every `executeRuling` for every dispute at once. Recoverable by governance, but it's a total halt of ruling delivery in the meantime.
- **Out of gas.** Vea's inbox appends to a Merkle tree, so `sendMessage` cost isn't constant — it depends on the trailing-ones pattern of the message count. Combined with the 63/64 rule, a caller who sized gas from a cheap estimate can OOG on an expensive append. Retry with more gas.
- **The inbox reverting on its own** — paused, retired, or a version mismatch after a Vea upgrade.
- **`arbitrationPaused`** blocks it at `:1145` before the call is even reached. Intentional, temporary.

**The structural gap:** `HomeGateway.changeVea` is a straight swap with no grace period — unlike `ForeignGateway.changeVea`, which keeps `deprecatedVeaOutbox` alive for a window on the inbound path. If the configured inbox ever becomes permanently unusable, there is no fallback route and no way to mark the dispute ruled by any other means. Nothing in the contract emits a signal on failure either, so the only evidence is a reverted tx that nobody may be watching for.

If you want the failure isolated so a stuck bridge can't hold the local dispute hostage, the fix is the same shape as concern #4 from the earlier review: wrap the `arbitrated.rule` call in `try/catch` with a gas stipend, record the ruling, and expose a separate permissionless "re-send to bridge" entry point.

content.text:
Good instinct to check, but the mechanism is the other way round from what you're describing — and that's worth pinning down precisely, because it changes which options are even on the table.

## The fee never crosses the bridge

Juror rewards on the home chain are funded by **the relayer's own money**, at relay time:

```
relayCreateDispute{value: msg.value}     // HomeGateway.sol:159 — relayer's ETH
  → KlerosCore.createDispute{value}      // :699  require(msg.value >= arbitrationCost)
      → _createDispute(..., msg.value)
          round.totalFeesForJurors = _feeAmount   // KlerosCore.sol:751
          round.nbVotes = _feeAmount / feeForJuror // :749
```

The pot is escrowed inside KlerosCore at creation, and `nbVotes` is *derived* from it, so a dispute cannot exist on the home chain with an underfunded reward pot — creation reverts first. Payout at `execute()` reads `round.totalFeesForJurors / numberOfVotesInRound` (`:923`) from that same escrowed amount.

Meanwhile the arbitrable's fee stays put in `ForeignGateway` and is used for exactly one thing: reimbursing the relayer at the very end via `withdrawFees` (`ForeignGateway.sol:232`). It is never bridged, never seen by KlerosCore, never touched by the reward logic.

So it's not a value bridge at all — it's closer to an **atomic swap with a multi-week settlement leg**. The relayer supplies home-chain liquidity now and claims foreign-chain liquidity later.

## Which means the reward logic can't break this way

- **Never relayed** → no dispute on the home chain at all. No jurors drawn, no rounds, nothing to pay. The reward logic isn't broken; it never runs. What's broken is that the arbitrable's fee is stranded on the foreign side with no refund path (the earlier concern #2).
- **Relayed, but the ruling never gets back** → jurors are paid in full. I confirmed last turn that `execute()` (`:909`) gates only on `Period.execution` and `whenNotPaused` and never reads `dispute.ruled`. Rewards, penalties and PNK unlocking all complete normally.

The exposure is entirely on the relayer: it's a **credit and liquidity risk, not a solvency risk**. Jurors are always made whole; the relayer is the one who may never be.

One thing that shrinks the problem: **appeals are not the relayer's concern.** `appeal()` is `payable` and sets `extraRound.totalFeesForJurors = msg.value` (`KlerosCore.sol:882`) from home-chain crowdfunders via the dispute kit. The relayer only ever fronts round 0. So the lock-up is `round-0 cost × disputes in flight`, not the full appeal-inflated amount.

## One thing that *does* look wrong, and it's fee-related

For the Gnosis pair, `HomeGatewayToGnosis` is deployed with **DAI** as `feeToken` (`deploy/02-home-gateway-to-gnosis.ts:28`), so KlerosCore charges `convertEthToTokenAmount(DAI, feeForJuror × minJurors)` — an ETH amount run through `RatesConverter.convert` (`RatesConverter.sol:73`). But `ForeignGatewayOnGnosis` collects native **xDAI**, and its mirror is seeded by copying the raw ETH-denominated value straight across:

```ts
const fee = (await core.courts(Courts.GENERAL)).feeForJuror;   // wei of ETH
await execute("ForeignGatewayOnGnosis", ..., "changeCourtJurorFee", Courts.GENERAL, fee);
```
`deploy/01-foreign-gateway-on-gnosis.ts:54-55`

That's an ETH-denominated number being used as an xDAI price — underpriced by roughly the ETH/DAI rate. The relayer would pay ~3000 DAI worth of fees on Arbitrum to be reimbursed ~1 xDAI on Gnosis. The Ethereum pair is fine (ETH on both sides, 1:1). These are the devnet/testnet scripts so mainnet may be configured by hand, but the mirror for a token-fee pair has to be maintained in *foreign native units at the current rate*, which is a second staleness surface on top of the one I flagged earlier, and nothing in the repo syncs either.

## Options other than fronting the fees

**1. Keep fronting, but actually price it.** Charge `cost × (1 + markup)` on the foreign side and pay the whole thing out at `withdrawFees`, plus add the timeout/refund path so the relayer's downside is bounded and the arbitrable can recover from a never-relayed dispute. Smallest diff, and it turns relaying from an act of charity into a business that someone other than Kleros can run. It does not remove the capital requirement.

**2. Prefunded home-chain float + batched sweep.** *This is the one I'd pursue.* Hold a vault on Arbitrum (treasury-seeded) that pays the arbitration cost inside `relayCreateDispute`. The relayer then needs **zero capital** — they submit the message and collect a gas reimbursement plus a small tip. Foreign-side fees accumulate in `ForeignGateway` and are swept to the home chain periodically, in bulk, off the critical path, amortizing bridge cost and latency.

The structural payoff is large: the per-dispute reimbursement machinery disappears entirely. `DisputeData.paid`, `DisputeData.relayer`, `withdrawFees`, and the `relayer` argument threaded through `relayRule` all go away — and with them the `.transfer()` gas trap (concern #6), the stranded-funds case (#2 becomes a governance sweep), and the scenario where a reverting arbitrable holds the relayer's principal hostage (#4). You trade a per-dispute cross-chain credit position for a float you have to keep topped up and account for.

**3. Move the value in the same message.** For Ethereum→Arbitrum this is genuinely available: an Arbitrum retryable ticket carries ETH *and* calldata atomically, in ~10 minutes, with no third party. That removes the relayer from the outbound leg entirely for that pair. But it doesn't generalise — Gnosis→Arbitrum has no canonical route, so you'd be back to a liquidity bridge with its own trust assumptions, and you'd lose the chain-agnostic shape the gateway currently has over Vea. Worth it only if Ethereum is the dominant pair.

**4. Stablecoin fee token on both sides.** Half-built already — `acceptedFeeTokens`, `RatesConverter` and the ERC20 `relayCreateDispute` overload all exist, and the DAI/xDAI choice for Gnosis shows the intent. It doesn't eliminate fronting, but it removes the relayer's multi-week price exposure and makes rebalancing cheap. Composes with option 1.

**5. Pay jurors from the foreign side after the ruling.** This is the literal reading of "don't relay the fees," and I'd reject it. KlerosCore derives `nbVotes` from the escrowed amount and locks juror PNK at draw time; an unfunded dispute means jurors stake collateral against an IOU that settles weeks later on another chain, contingent on a bridge working. That converts a bounded relayer credit risk into an unbounded juror credit risk spread across every participant, and it needs invasive changes to core. Wrong direction.

**Recommendation:** 2 + 1 together. The float makes the hot path capital-free and genuinely permissionless, the markup and timeout bound what's left, and you delete a meaningful chunk of the bug surface from the earlier review as a side effect. Do the Gnosis fee-denomination check first regardless of which path you take — it's independent and it's live.

content.text:
Here's what I'd actually build.

## Two rules

**1. `ForeignGateway` should never hold funds.** Every problem in this area traces back to the fee sitting on the wrong chain for weeks, earmarked to a party who may never be able to claim it. If the balance is always zero, `withdrawFees`, `DisputeData.paid`, `DisputeData.relayer`, the `_relayer` parameter on `relayRule`, and the whole stranded-funds class disappear.

**2. Separate pricing from funding.** Today they're the same number: the foreign quote *is* the relayer's reimbursement. So a stale mirror doesn't just misprice — it silently converts into a relayer loss or an unrelayable dispute. These should be two independent mechanisms with independent failure modes.

## Target: let the fee ride the canonical deposit

The key asymmetry nobody's exploiting: **the two legs go in opposite directions and have opposite cost profiles.**

- Ruling, Arbitrum → L1, is a *withdrawal*: 7 days canonically. That's precisely why Vea exists. Keep Vea here.
- Dispute creation, L1 → Arbitrum, is a *deposit*: ~10 minutes, canonical, trustless — **and a retryable ticket carries ETH and calldata together.**

So for the Ethereum pair, `ForeignGateway.createDispute` shouldn't emit an event and sit on the money. It should call the Arbitrum Delayed Inbox with `l2CallValue = arbitrationCost` and the `relayCreateDispute` calldata. The fee lands on Arbitrum as actual value in the same operation that creates the dispute, and funds `round.totalFeesForJurors` directly.

What that buys you:

- **No relayer on the outbound leg.** No capital fronting, no reimbursement claim, no multi-week credit exposure, no tip to price.
- **Authentication for free.** `HomeGateway` checks `AddressAliasHelper.applyL1ToL2Alias(foreignGateway) == msg.sender` instead of re-deriving a hash from parameters an untrusted bot typed in. Short answer: **no, not as the contract stands** — and the reason it's blocked is more interesting than the obvious `require`.

## Three things block it, not one

**1. The gate.** `require(msg.value >= arbitrationCost(_extraData))` at `KlerosCore.sol:699`. Trivially removable, and it's the only one people usually notice.

**2. The jury size is derived from the money.** `round.nbVotes = _feeAmount / feeForJuror` (`:749`). Pass zero and you get a dispute with zero jurors — `draw` finds nothing to do, and `execute()` computes `round.totalFeesForJurors / numberOfVotesInRound` where `numberOfVotesInRound = round.drawnJurors.length` (`:922-923`), i.e. `0 / 0`, which panics. The dispute isn't merely unfunded, it's permanently unexecutable. You'd have to re-derive `nbVotes` from `minJurors` instead, and then reconcile the fact that the fee no longer determines the jury size.

**3. There is no per-dispute escrow.** This is the one that actually matters. `_transferFeeToken` (`:1419`) pays out of KlerosCore's **commingled balance**. `round.totalFeesForJurors` is a bookkeeping cap, not a segregated pot — `_executeRewards` clamps against it at `:1088-1090`, but the tokens themselves come from whatever the contract happens to hold.

So an unfunded dispute wouldn't fail loudly. It would **pay its jurors out of other disputes' escrowed fees**, settle perfectly, and push the deficit onto some unrelated dispute weeks later — surfacing as a failed transfer in an innocent party's `execute()`, or quietly eating the `leftoverFeeReward` that would otherwise go to `owner` at `:1129`. There's no liability tracking and no solvency invariant anywhere in the contract to catch it.

That's the real answer to your question: deferring payment isn't a timing change, it converts KlerosCore from fully-escrowed to fractional-reserve, and none of the accounting that would require exists.

There's a fourth, softer problem: jurors are exposed from *draw* time, not payment time. `draw` calls `sortitionModule.lockStake(drawnAddress, round.pnkAtStakePerJuror)` (`:835`), and penalties at `:1001` apply regardless of whether any fee ever arrives. PNK rewards are self-funding (they come from incoherent jurors' penalties), but fee rewards aren't. So an unfunded dispute means jurors lock capital and can be penalized with no guaranteed upside.

## What you probably actually want: prepaid, not deferred

Keep the escrow invariant — core is always fully funded at creation — but change *whose pocket* and *when the top-up happens*. Give the gateway a balance inside KlerosCore and debit it in `_createDispute` instead of reading `msg.value`.

The gating primitive is already there: `arbitrableWhitelist` / `arbitrableWhitelistEnabled` (`:117-118`, checked at `:730`). Add a per-arbitrable prepaid balance alongside it, and `relayCreateDispute` becomes a balance debit rather than a value transfer. From the relayer's point of view the dispute is created without anyone paying at that moment; from core's point of view nothing changed at all. Top-ups happen in bulk, off the critical path.

That's a small, well-contained core change, it preserves every existing invariant, and it gets you the property you're after.

## The one version of "create first, pay later" I'd consider sound

If you genuinely want the dispute to exist before the money does, the only safe shape is to **separate existence from the draw**: a `funding` state where the dispute has an ID (so the cross-chain hash binding works and evidence can be submitted) but no jurors are drawn and no PNK is locked. Nothing is at risk while unfunded. Fee arrives → `nbVotes` computed, draw proceeds. Timeout → cancel cleanly.

But be clear-eyed about what that buys you for the gateway: **it doesn't remove the need for the fee to reach Arbitrum before jurors can be drawn.** It only moves *when* you need the bridge to have worked, not *whether*. Its real benefit is that an unrelayable dispute fails cleanly instead of stranding funds — and you can get exactly that property far more cheaply with a timeout refund on the foreign side, without touching core at all.

So: prepaid balance for the funding problem, timeout refund for the failure problem. I wouldn't build deferred funding into core for this.

Hashi changes the calculus in one important way that's easy to miss, and I'd build around it.

## What Hashi gives you, and what it takes away

**Takes away:** value can never ride the message. Yaho/Yaru move bytes, nothing else. So "let the fee travel with the dispute on the canonical bridge" — the thing I'd have pushed for the Ethereum pair — is off the table everywhere. Fees stay on the foreign chain by construction.

**Gives you:** the outbound leg can finally be *authenticated*. Today dispute creation isn't a message at all — it's an off-chain bot re-typing parameters into a hash on the other side, with no proof. With Hashi you can dispatch `ForeignGateway → Yaho → Yaru → HomeGateway` and have the home side know, under N-of-M, that the foreign gateway really did collect a fee for exactly these parameters.

That second point is what unlocks the fee design. Under Vea I was reluctant about a home-chain float because nothing proved the foreign payment happened, so the vault was drainable and needed bonds or a whitelist to gate it. With an authenticated creation message, **the float's solvency is protected by the bridge's own security** — draining it requires forging N-of-M, which is the same assumption everything else already rests on. The bond, the whitelist and the relayer-reimbursement machinery all become unnecessary.

## The architecture I'd aim for

Three rails that never touch each other per-dispute:

1. **Messages** — Hashi, both directions. Creation *and* ruling.
2. **Value** — one canonical fee asset, same on every chain, moved in batches on its own schedule.
3. **Execution** — whoever calls `Yaru.executeMessages` gets a gas reimbursement. A gas job, not a capital job.

Fee flow becomes: arbitrable pays on the foreign chain → fee sits there as protocol revenue → creation message arrives on Arbitrum → HomeGateway funds the dispute from the float → jurors paid from escrow as normal → foreign balances swept periodically to top the float back up.

No per-dispute cross-chain claim exists anywhere. `DisputeData.paid`, `DisputeData.relayer`, `withdrawFees` and the `_relayer` parameter all delete.

## The single biggest lever: stop denominating fees in native currency

This is where multi-chain either works or doesn't. Today the mirror is `feeForJuror` in the foreign chain's native unit — which is why the Gnosis deploy is quoting an ETH number as an xDAI price. At two chains that's a bug. At eight chains it's N independent price feeds, N drift surfaces, and N illiquid rebalancing paths, and nobody can hold that in their head.

**Denominate the fee in one asset that exists natively on every chain you support — USDC is the obvious pick, and CCTP gives you trust-minimized rebalancing that doesn't touch Hashi at all.**

What that buys:

- `feeForJuror` becomes **one number, identical on every foreign chain**. No per-chain rate, no per-chain mirror, no per-chain drift. The whole bug class from the earlier review disappears rather than being fixed N times.
- Core already supports it — `acceptedFeeTokens`, `RatesConverter`, `round.feeToken`, and the ERC20 `relayCreateDispute` overload all exist. You'd be finishing a path that's half-built, not inventing one.
- Reimbursement and sweeps are USDC→USDC. No FX exposure over a multi-week dispute, which is the thing that makes the current relayer model unviable past one or two chains.
- Juror rewards land in USDC. That's a product decision, not a technical one, but stable juror income is arguably an improvement. If you need to keep jurors in ETH, keep core's internal `feeForJuror` in ETH and let `RatesConverter` produce the USDC quote — you still end up with **one** rate to maintain instead of N.

Hard constraint that falls out: only support chains where the canonical fee asset exists natively. A chain without it needs its own rate and its own liquidity, and should be treated as a second-class integration with an explicit multiplier, not folded into the general path.

## Fee sync becomes a broadcast

`HomeGateway.syncCourtFee(courtID)` dispatches the same payload to every registered chain through Yaho. Permissionless to trigger, authenticated on arrival by Yaru plus an expected-sender check. Because the payload is identical everywhere, there's no per-chain configuration to drift.

Then **fail closed**: the foreign gateway rejects `createDispute` if its last sync is older than some max age. At eight chains you cannot manually watch eight mirrors, and a stale mirror quoting a too-low price is exactly how you get unfundable disputes. A revert is recoverable; a bad quote isn't.

## Two new cost lines the fee has to cover

Worth pricing explicitly, because neither existed under Vea:

- **N adapter relays per message.** Hashi's cost scales with the adapter set. The ruling leg now costs N relays instead of one subsidized Vea relay, and if creation also goes over Hashi, that's 2N per dispute. This needs to be in the quote, not absorbed.
- **Per-chain risk.** Different chains will run different adapter sets and thresholds, so they genuinely have different security and different latency. A `chainMultiplier[chainId]` on top of the global court fee is the one place per-chain config is justified — and it gives you a dial to price a weak adapter set honestly rather than cross-subsidizing it from strong chains.

## The acceptance test for "seamless"

Adding chain N+1 should require exactly: deploy `ForeignGateway`, register its adapter set in ShoyuBashi, add it to the home dispatch list, point it at the local canonical USDC, set its risk multiplier. **No new price feed, no new fee denomination, no new relayer liquidity pool, no new bot.** If a proposed design fails that test, it won't survive past three or four chains.

## What I'd nail down first

The one real tradeoff is **creation latency**. Routing creation through Hashi means waiting for N-of-M instead of a bot acting in seconds. For arbitration that's probably fine — an extra hour against a multi-week dispute, though it does delay the evidence period. If it turns out to matter, the hybrid is a bonded relayer creating immediately on an optimistic fast path, with the Hashi message arriving later to settle the float and slash on mismatch. That works, but it reintroduces bonds and fraud proofs, so I'd only take it if you measure the latency as an actual problem.

Second thing to settle early: whether jurors get paid in USDC. It gates whether core's internal denomination changes or only the external quote does, and everything else is easier to sequence once that's decided.
